newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa faces capacity challenge - Mandela.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa faces capacity challenge - Mandela.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela said on Tuesday South Africa's economy was growing and delivery to the victims of apartheid was accelerating, but improving the way in which the country was run posed a serious challenge.
"Recent economic indicators continue to provide compelling evidence that structural changes have indeed put us on the path to sustained economic growth.
"Whether it be productivity, export performance, utilisation of capacity or fixed investment, the prognosis for the long term improves by the month," he told parliament.
Introducing a routine annual debate on his budget, Mandela -- who marks three years in power on May 10 -- identified crime, training and national unity as priorities.
He said the ability to deliver the services and infrastructure South Africa needed to overcome the backlogs created by centuries of white rule remained a major challenge.
"While the budget spells out our choices as a nation and helps us toward their realisation, achieving them depends on our own actions.

"In particular, success will elude us unless we frankly and urgently address the serious capacity problems we face in the civil service, in the criminal justice system, in our provinces and local authorities, in our economy," he said.

Amongst the achievements of South Africa's first democratic government, Mandela listed the provision of fresh water to more than one million people, electricity for 1.5 million households, the construction of 400 clinics and awarding almost 500,000 housing subsidies linked to land and services.
"The message is clear: The lives of millions have begun to change and the pace of delivery is accelerating," he said.
Mandela's government is facing increasing criticism from blacks disappointed by the limited improvement in their lives since apartheid ended with his election in April 1994.
Ministers argue, however, that the former government had never addressed the needs of the black majority and that no capacity existed to extend services to them.
Mandela said the macroeconomic strategy for growth, employment and redistribution published in June last year was starting to bear fruit.

"In our actions to invest in human resources, in the building of the economy and entrenching safety and security and in democratising the state, we are slowly but surely achieving the reconstruction and development of our country," he said.
